Altmann and Kamide (1999) provided early evidence of this latter possibility in the VWP: participants were asked to passively listen to sentences containing verbs which occasionally constrained for an upcoming direct object.
However, despite this apparent automaticity, predictive effects emerged earlier when participants had received the metalinguistic judgement task.

Using the honorific marker, Kim et al. (2026) argued that listeners could generate predictions about the upcoming referent (e.g., teacher in the honorific condition, young man in the nonhonorific condition) and so would display earlier and more frequent anticipatory fixations to the relevant referent (see Kim et al., 2024, for proof of concept). Kim et al. (2026) also manipulated the task relevance of the honorific cue: some participants were asked to listen to each sentence and respond to a question about the referent while others were told to actively predict the upcoming referent.

We recruited 135 participants by word-of-mouth and from the departments of Spanish and Portuguese Studies; Speech, Language, and Hearing Sciences; and Linguistics at the University of Florida.
Participants were required to have no issues with hearing, seeing, learning, or reading.
Eight participants were excluded because their eye movements could not be tracked or their data could not be extracted.
Two participants were excluded from analysis due to not fitting the language background criteria of the experiment.

Three participants were dropped for poor-quality of eye-tracking data resulting in fewer than six usable trials in either the predictive or non-predictive conditions, 1 participant was excluded for a lack of fixations in the interest areas during the predictive window, and 1 participant was removed for failing to meet the preregistered minimum for comprehension accuracy (80%).
Additionally, participants were grouped according to a betweengroup attention task.
Participants were instructed to attend to either the actions of the Male (Male-attending) or Female referent (Female-attending) and answer referent-specific questions for comprehension.

Male-attending participants were instructed to listen to the actions of the Male referent and answer a corresponding comprehension question after each trial (e.g., What did Gary answer?) ; Female-attending participants were similarly instructed and received relevant post-trial questions (e.g., What did Mary produce?).
We recruited 48 participants (age: 19 to 66, M = 33.9) on Prolific (https://www.prolific.com/) with a minimum approval rate of 80%.

Participants were then asked to select which picture was most likely to be mentioned next in the sentence fragment.
Items and conditions were randomized for each participant, and three attention checks (e.g., Please select the fridge) were presented randomly.
Participants were shown 68 trials in total.
Participants were seated approximately 60 cm away from a 27-inch computer monitor with their forehead and chin on a desk-mounted headrest to minimize movement.
Participants completed a 9-point calibration and validation procedure for the collection of accurate horizontal and vertical eyemovements.
Prior to the experiment, participants were given oral and written instructions that they would be listening to sentences while looking at objects displayed on the screen in front of them.
Participants were also instructed to attend to the actions of either the Male or the Female referent in each sentence and answer a corresponding comprehension question after each trial.
Participants were also able to take a break halfway through the experiment.

After the experiment, participants completed a debriefing survey and language background questionnaire via Google Forms (responses to both forms for Experiments 1 and 2 can be found on OSF; osf.io/63xr2).
All participants gave written informed consent; per regulations and policies of the Institutional Review Board of the University of Florida, the experimental protocol was exempt from review.

In total, 120 unique participants were included in the final analysis.

One potential reason for the lack of difference between the attention groups is that Female-attending participants were strategically attending to the Male referent in order to rule out the target object as a valid comprehension question answer and so converge more rapidly on the relevant object.

Crucially, these participants were given an explicit instruction task to predict, rather than simply pay attention to, the actions of the Male referent; thus, the task relevance of prediction was made explicit in Experiment 2.
To further ensure participants were maximally aware of prediction's task relevance, we also asked participants to report the accuracy and confidence of their trial-by-trial predictions.

Across two eye-tracking experiments, we examined whether the extent and onset of predictive processing is sensitive to the task relevance of a predictive cue when participants are given an attention task that renders said cue relevant or irrelevant (RQ1) or an explicit task to engage in prediction (RQ2).
In Experiment 1, the task relevance of a predictive verbal cue varied based on the referent participants were instructed to attend to.
Consequently, our participants may have been uniquely advantaged in knowing where and when to predict and so may have been able to initiate prediction earlier.
table.header: Effects of explicit manipulations of task relevance

table.text: If participants are given an attentional demand akin to Experiment 1 but are expected to predict from the perspective of a referent within the stimuli, task relevance effects may emerge in the form of reduced and delayed predictive fixations.

Similarly, target window effects from Experiment 2, where explicitly instructed participants were less likely to fixate the target noun when it was not cued for by the verb, suggest that specifying task relevance can have downstream consequences for the integration of unpredictable information or stimuli which do not immediately fit into the task-demands (cf. power.title: Power Analysis Check

table.text: Three participants were dropped for poor-quality of eye-tracking data resulting in fewer than six usable trials in either the predictive or non-predictive conditions, 1 participant was excluded for a lack of fixations in the interest areas during the predictive window, and 1 participant was removed for failing to meet the preregistered minimum for comprehension accuracy (80%). Our preregistered analysis called for 120 participants; this number was chosen on the basis of similar sample sizes in adjacent research, as well as a preregistered power analysis estimate necessary to reach 80% power for an interaction of our factors. Ultimately, 120 participants (age: M = 20.1, SD = 1.36) were included in the final analysis, with 57 in the Male-attending (33 self-identified as female; age: M = 20, SD = 1.1) and 63 in the Female-attending (38 self-identified as female; 2 self-identified as nonbinary; age: M = 20.1, SD = 1.56) condition. All participants received compensation in the form of either course credit or cash at a rate of $5.00 USD per 0.5 hours.

table.title: Attention and Prediction: An Eye-tracking Study
table.data_collection_started: No, no data have been collected for this study yet.
table.research_questions: Is predictive processing during listening affected by attention? In particular, do listeners move their eyes to a predicted object on the screen faster / to a larger extent when the predictive cue (verb) and predicted object are task-relevant than when they are not?
table.design_dependent_variables:
The position of the eye will be recorded at a sampling rate of 1000 Hz, down sampled to 20 Hz. Looks to the target object image and the two distractor images will be defined as fixations within a rectangle tightly fitting the entire object image on the screen.  
For critical window analysis discussed below, we will look at the total number of bins with fixations to the target object vs. the total number of bins with fixations to distractors within the predictive time window. This duration of this window corresponds to the average interval between the onset of the verb and the onset of the noun (“average_interval_duration”). We will time-lock to the noun onset. The predictive time window is then defined as ranging from ( time_of_noun_onset  - average_interval_duration + 200 ms) to  (time_of_noun_onset + 200 ms).
table.study_design_overview:
This study has a 2 (predictive/neutral) x 2 (attention group) design.  All participants listen to sentences of two types illustrated in 1a and 1b.

Predictive verb	
1a. After John answered his phone, Mary sighed and produced her wallet 	(images: Phone Wallet Keys)	
Neutral verb
1b. After John lost his phone, Mary sighed and produced her wallet	(images: Phone Wallet Keys)	


In the predictive version of the sentence (1a), the first verb (answer) is predictive of one of the three objects in the display; in the neutral version (1b), the first verb (lost) can be used with any of the three objects. In the experimental sentences, the first verb in the sentence always has a male referent as agent (John), the second verb in the sentence always has a female agent (Mary). The attentional manipulation will be between-group. Half of the participants will be randomly assigned to group A, half to group B. Group A will be told to pay attention to what male referents are doing and systematically receive questions about male referents; Group B will be told to pay attention to what female referents and will always be asked about female agents. Examples are given below of the questions following 1a/b:

Comprehension question Group A (always about male referents; first clause in critical items)
What did John answer/lose? (phone/wallet/keys)	
Comprehension question Group B (always about female referents; second clause in critical items)
What did Mary produce? (phone/wallet/keys)


Participants will be randomly assigned to Group A or Group B. To reduce strategizing, the distractor items in the study will have female referents paired with the first verb in the sentence, and male referents with the second sentence. We expect that this attentional manipulation will affect the eye-movements starting at the first verb, with people in the A group moving their eyes more often or more quickly to the target “phone” when the first verb is predictive (1a,  vs. neutral 1b) compared to participants in the B-group.
table.statistical_tests: To test whether group A shows more target fixations than group B in the predictive time window, we will use as DV the number of bins with target fixations (vs. bins with fixations to distractors) in the time window as defined above. If these data are unimodally distributed without a substantial skew we use the proportion of bins with looks as dependent measure; otherwise we will use (weighted) empirical logits as dependent measure.    We will use (generalized) linear mixed effects models (lme4 in R). Condition (deviation coded), group (deviation coded) and their interaction will be entered as fixed effects. The random effects include by-subject and by-item intercepts. We will start with a maximal model as justified by the design. If such a model does not converge, we will take out the random effects with the smallest variance until the model converges without warnings. Interactions will be resolved by recoding the effects such that one of the groups or one of the conditions is the reference level; effects of condition or group, respectively then are the effects for the group or condition at the reference level.
table.outliers_and_exclusions:
Participant in/exclusion criteria
Participants will be included if:
- they grew up speaking English at home in a predominantly English speaking country and learned English before the age of 6, and are still comfortable speaking English
- they are between the ages of 18 -35
-they do not have any self-reported problems with hearing, vision, reading or learning

Participants’ data will be excluded from analysis if:
-	They have fewer than 80% correct answers to the comprehension questions
-	If they have 5 or fewer useable trials left for one or both conditions (see data point exclusion below)

Data point exclusion criteria
Data points will be excluded if the sample point contains blinks, saccades, or tracker loss
Trials will be excluded that contain less than 50% useable data points in the critical time window
Trials with incorrect answer to the comprehension question
table.sample_size:
We will collect 60 useable data sets per group, 120 in total. In case we experience financial, time, or practical constraints, we may need to stop the study before these numbers are reached. Each participant will get 16 items per condition. The number of 120 participants is based on the typical group size in recent VWP studies (e.g. Lago et al. 2021). In addition, a power analysis suggested a similar number of participants to obtain 80% power for the group x condition interaction. 
Power estimates were based on VWP eyetracking data from Lago et al. (2022) Experiment 1. This study compared two groups on a condition manipulation with 4 objects in the display. We used these data to make a model including only by-subjects and by-item random-intercepts: glmer(TargetAdvantage (note1) ~ cGroup * cCondition + (1|SubjectID) + (1|ItemID), family = binomial). The coefficient of the group x condition interaction was around .2 on the basis of the Lago et al. data. 
In addition, we derived estimates of coefficients from Altmann and Kamide (1999). Altmann and Kamide report two VWP experiments using a predictive and a non-predictive verb. In experiment 1, participants had  to click on objects mentioned; in experiment 2 participants were asked just to listen for comprehension. This roughly corresponds to our attention manipulation and experimental design. Based on the percentages of looks reported in the predictive region to the target and to the distractors, we estimated the following coefficients:  intercept .6; effect of attention 0.1; effect of prediction: 0.4; attention x prediction: 0.2. We then used the mixedpower package in R, the model above, and the Lago et al. Exp.1 data to estimate the power for different subject numbers on the basis of these new coefficients, and 32 items.  Power for the interaction was .81 for 120 participants, based on 1,000 simulations.

table.additional_comments: We will conduct a divergence point analysis (Stone et al. 2019) as an exploratory analysis to (1) obtain the confidence interval of the onset of predictive looks to the target for each group separately; (2) to assess whether the groups differ in the divergence point.

table.research_questions:
Is predictive processing during listening affected by attention? In particular, do listeners move their eyes to a predictable object on the screen faster / to a larger extent when explicitly asked to predict than when they are not?   
This study is a follow-up of the study preregistered on https://osf.io/6qfcg
table.design_dependent_variables:
Similar to the prior study, the position of the eye will be recorded at a sampling rate of 1000 Hz, down sampled to 20 Hz. Looks to the target object image and the two distractor images will be defined as fixations within a rectangle tightly fitting the entire object image on the screen. 
For the critical window analysis discussed below, we will look at the total number of bins with fixations to the target object vs. the total number of bins with fixations to distractors within the predictive time window. This duration of this window corresponds to the average interval between the onset of the verb and the onset of the noun (“average_interval_duration”). We will time-lock to the noun onset. The predictive time window is then defined as ranging from ( time_of_noun_onset  - average_interval_duration + 200 ms) to  (time_of_noun_onset + 200 ms).
table.study_design_overview:
Materials (sentences and displays) are identical to the prior study. In this follow-up study, as in the prior study, all participants listen to sentences of two types illustrated in 1a and 1b. In the predictive version of the sentence (1a), the first verb (answer) is predictive of one of the three objects in the display; in the neutral version (1b), the first verb (lost) can be used with any of the three objects. In the experimental sentences, the first verb in the sentence always has a male referent as agent (John), the second verb in the sentence always has a female agent (Mary). To reduce strategizing, the distractor items in the study will have female referents paired with the first verb in the sentence, and male referents with the second sentence.

Predictive verb 1a. After John answered his phone, Mary sighed and produced her wallet (images: Phone Wallet Keys)

Neutral verb 1b. After John lost his phone, Mary sighed and produced her wallet (images: Phone Wallet Keys)

In this follow-up study, all participants will systematically receive questions about male referents (like Group A in the prior study):

Comprehension Question: What did John answer/lose? (images: Phone/Wallet/Keys)

Unlike in the prior study, participants in this follow-up study will be explicitly instructed to predict what object the male character will engage with. At the end of the trial, participants get the comprehension question, and will be asked whether their prediction was correct/incorrect and how confident they were in their predictions on a scale of 1 (not sure at all) to 5 (very certain).
These data will be compared with the prior study, in which attention was manipulated between two groups. The first group (A) was told to pay attention to what male referents are doing and systematically received questions about male referents; the second group (B) was told to pay attention to what female referents and will always be asked about female agents. 
We expect that the explicit prediction instructions in the current study will affect the eye-movements starting at the first verb, with people in the current study moving their eyes more often or more quickly to the target “phone” when the first verb is predictive (1a vs. neutral 1b) compared to participants in the initial study.
table.statistical_tests: We will primarily compare data from the current group with the group in the prior study who was asked to pay attention to the male characters (Group A). The difference in the instructions between the groups is that the current group receives explicit prediction instructions. To test whether the current group shows more target fixations than the prior group in the predictive time window, we will use as DV the number of bins with target fixations (vs. bins with fixations to distractors) in the time window as defined above. If these data are unimodally distributed without a substantial skew we use the proportion of bins with looks as dependent measure; otherwise we will use (weighted) empirical logits as dependent measure.  We will use (generalized) linear mixed effects models (lme4 in R). Condition (deviation coded), Group (deviation coded, Group A vs. current group) and their interaction will be entered as fixed effects. The random effects include by-subject and by-item intercepts. We will start with a maximal model as justified by the design. If such a model does not converge, we will take out the random effects with the smallest variance until the model converges without warnings. Interactions will be resolved by recoding the effects such that one of the groups or one of the conditions is the reference level; effects of condition or group, respectively then are the effects for the group or condition at the reference level.

- they grew up speaking English at home in a predominantly English speaking country and learned English before the age of 6, and are still comfortable speaking English
- they are between the ages of 18 -35
-they do not have any self-reported problems with hearing, vision, reading or learning

Participants’ data will be excluded from analysis if:
-	They have fewer than 80% correct answers to the comprehension questions
-	If they have 5 or fewer useable trials left for one or both conditions (see data point exclusion below)

Data point exclusion criteria:
Data points will be excluded if the sample point contains blinks, saccades, or tracker loss
Trials will be excluded that contain less than 50% useable data points in the critical time window
Trials with incorrect answer to the comprehension question
table.sample_size: We will collect 60 usable data sets.  In case we experience financial, time, or practical constraints, we may need to stop the study before these numbers are reached. Each participant will get 16 items per condition. The number of 60 participants is based on the group size in the prior study. See https://osf.io/6qfcg for motivation.
table.additional_comments:
We will conduct a divergence point analysis (Stone et al. 2019) as an exploratory analysis to (1) obtain the confidence interval of the onset of predictive looks to the target for each group separately; (2) to assess whether the groups differ in the divergence point.
In addition, we explore the difference between the current group and the group in the prior study that was instructed to pay attention to the female characters (Group B). These groups will differ maximally in the task-relevance of the critical object.
We will also explore to what extent the self-reported correctness of and confidence in the prediction affects predictive eye movements.

#### Files that do not belong in the repository

We left out 10 files that software creates by itself, not the authors: operating system (10). They hold nothing a reader can use, but they clutter the repository, and software can mistake them for real files (for example a `._` copy of a `.csv` for data).

*Remove these:* *Operating system* files: macOS adds a `__MACOSX` folder and a `._` copy of every file it puts in a zip, and `.DS_Store` files to folders; Windows adds `Thumbs.db` and `desktop.ini`. On a Mac, create zips from the command line with `zip -r -X`, or remove them afterwards with `zip -d archive.zip "__MACOSX/*" "*.DS_Store"`. *RStudio session files* (`.Rproj.user/`) hold open tabs and unsaved edits; *R history* (`.Rhistory`) lists the commands typed in a session and can hold file paths and passwords; *Jupyter checkpoints* (`.ipynb_checkpoints/`) are automatic copies of notebooks; *compiled Python files* (`__pycache__/`, `.pyc`) are recreated when the code runs; *open-document lock files* (`~$...docx`, `.~lock...#`) are left while a document is open; *editor backups* (`file~`, `.bak`, `.swp`) and *temporary files* (`.tmp`, `.temp`) are copies a program made by itself.

*Keep only on purpose:* *version control* folders (`.git`, `.svn`, `.hg`) hold the project's history, which can include earlier versions of files and data that was later removed; *editor settings* (`.idea`, `.vscode`) can hold paths on your own computer. A `.gitignore` based on GitHub's templates (https://github.com/github/gitignore) keeps them out of a repository.

This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.
We examined 88 columns across 3 data files.
#### Issues Identified

48 file/column combinations have at least one issue.

**About the personal-information flags.** These are pattern matches, not confirmed disclosures, and they are tuned to over-report rather than miss something. Expect false positives:

- **Column names** are matched against identifying words in English and other European languages (`email`, `telefoonnummer`, `geboortedatum`, ...). A column called `phone_number` flags whether or not it holds one, and an empty or already-anonymised column flags on its name alone.
- **Values** are matched against the shape of an identifier. An IP address pattern also matches a version string or a dotted numeric code; a card-number pattern requires both a real issuer prefix and a checksum, but a long numeric ID can still coincide.
- **Free text** is flagged when a column holds long, mostly-distinct prose — the shape open-ended answers take. Most such columns contain no names at all.

A flag means *look at this column*. Where the data is already de-identified (an `ip` column reading `Anonymized`, a `name` column the authors emptied), no action is needed.

#### Careless Responding

116 distinct respondents were flagged for **straightlining**: giving the same answer for at least 80% of the items in a multi-item scale of 5 items or more. One respondent can be flagged in several scales; the table below is **one row per person**, and the *Longest run* column gives the run that triggered the strongest flag, so you can check it against the raw data.

Of these, **116 were flagged *only* by short-scale straightlining** (a run of identical answers on a scale of 7 items or fewer). On a short, one-directional scale, answering consistently is often normal, coherent responding rather than carelessness — treat these as weak signals and inspect the actual responses before excluding anyone.
These are prompts to inspect those rows, not definitive judgements.

Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

(2026) argued that listeners could generate predictions about the upcoming referent (e.g., teacher in the honorific condition, young man in the nonhonorific condition) and so would display earlier and more frequent anticipatory fixations to the relevant referent (see Kim et al., 2024, for proof of concept). Kim et al. (2026) also manipulated the task relevance of the honorific cue: some participants were asked to listen to each sentence and respond to a question about the referent while others were told to actively predict the upcoming referent.

In the first study, some participants were given an explicit prediction task ("predict how the sentence [is] likely to continue", p. 811) before receiving a comprehension task for a different set of stimuli.

Based on anticipatory fixations, Ito (2025) found that participants were more likely to fixate an upcoming target object which was constrained for by the verb, and that they were more likely to do so when there was an explicit prediction task.

However, there was a main effect of task such that participants were more likely to fixate a target in the explicit prediction condition even when the verb was not predictive of the target. Ito (2025) thus argued that the benefit of explicit prediction tasks for predictive processing is general, with listeners using top-down strategies to upregulate predictive visual search rather than to "enhance prediction at their will" (p. 822).

Thus, by manipulating the referent to whom participants were instructed to attend, we also established a proxy manipulation of task relevance, with the predictive cue being taskirrelevant for participants attending to the Female referent.
We recruited 135 participants by word-of-mouth and from the departments of Spanish and Portuguese Studies; Speech, Language, and Hearing Sciences; and Linguistics at the University of Florida.
Participants were required to have no issues with hearing, seeing, learning, or reading.
Eight participants were excluded because their eye movements could not be tracked or their data could not be extracted.
Two participants were excluded from analysis due to not fitting the language background criteria of the experiment.

Three participants were dropped for poor-quality of eye-tracking data resulting in fewer than six usable trials in either the predictive or non-predictive conditions, 1 participant was excluded for a lack of fixations in the interest areas during the predictive window, and 1 participant was removed for failing to meet the preregistered minimum for comprehension accuracy (80%).
Additionally, participants were grouped according to a betweengroup attention task.
Participants were instructed to attend to either the actions of the Male (Male-attending) or Female referent (Female-attending) and answer referent-specific questions for comprehension.

Male-attending participants were instructed to listen to the actions of the Male referent and answer a corresponding comprehension question after each trial (e.g., What did Gary answer?) ; Female-attending participants were similarly instructed and received relevant post-trial questions (e.g., What did Mary produce?).
We recruited 48 participants (age: 19 to 66, M = 33.9) on Prolific (https://www.prolific.com/) with a minimum approval rate of 80%.
This approval rate was chosen to screen for participant quality and excluded participants rejected from more than 20% of Prolific studies they have participated in.
Participants were then asked to select which picture was most likely to be mentioned next in the sentence fragment.
Items and conditions were randomized for each participant, and three attention checks (e.g., Please select the fridge) were presented randomly.
Participants were shown 68 trials in total.
Participants were seated approximately 60 cm away from a 27-inch computer monitor with their forehead and chin on a desk-mounted headrest to minimize movement.
Participants completed a 9-point calibration and validation procedure for the collection of accurate horizontal and vertical eyemovements.
Prior to the experiment, participants were given oral and written instructions that they would be listening to sentences while looking at objects displayed on the screen in front of them.
Participants were also instructed to attend to the actions of either the Male or the Female referent in each sentence and answer a corresponding comprehension question after each trial.
Participants were also able to take a break halfway through the experiment.

After the experiment, participants completed a debriefing survey and language background questionnaire via Google Forms (responses to both forms for Experiments 1 and 2 can be found on OSF; osf.io/63xr2).
All participants gave written informed consent; per regulations and policies of the Institutional Review Board of the University of Florida, the experimental protocol was exempt from review.

Finally, we excluded participants who had fewer than six usable trials across either level of Condition (three participants, all of whom were Female-attending), participants who had less than 80% accuracy on the comprehension questions (one participant, Male-attending), as well as participants who did not meet our inclusion criteria (two participants, both Female-attending).
In total, 120 unique participants were included in the final analysis.
Hence, participants were paying attention to their assigned referent.

There was also a main effect of Attention Group: Maleattending participants were more likely to fixate the target object within the target window than the Female-attending participants, b = 0.459, SE = 0.169, z = 2.728, p < 0.01.
Participants were given an attention task that determined whether a predictive verbal cue was task-relevant (Male-attending) or task-irrelevant (Female-attending).

One potential reason for the lack of difference between the attention groups is that Female-attending participants were strategically attending to the Male referent in order to rule out the target object as a valid comprehension question answer and so converge more rapidly on the relevant object.

Crucially, these participants were given an explicit instruction task to predict, rather than simply pay attention to, the actions of the Male referent; thus, the task relevance of prediction was made explicit in Experiment 2.
To further ensure participants were maximally aware of prediction's task relevance, we also asked participants to report the accuracy and confidence of their trial-by-trial predictions.
All participants provided informed consent; per regulations and policies of the Institutional Review Board of the University of Florida, the experimental protocol was exempt from review.

6 One participant who failed to meet the exclusion criteria was then excluded (Explicit Prediction task), as was one participant who had less than 80% accuracy on comprehension questions (Attention task) and one participant with no looks to any interest area in the predictive window (Attention task).
Following pre-processing, a total of 117 participants were included in the final analysis comparing Experiments 1 and 2.

Across two eye-tracking experiments, we examined whether the extent and onset of predictive processing is sensitive to the task relevance of a predictive cue when participants are given an attention task that renders said cue relevant or irrelevant (RQ1) or an explicit task to engage in prediction (RQ2).
In Experiment 1, the task relevance of a predictive verbal cue varied based on the referent participants were instructed to attend to.
Consequently, our participants may have been uniquely advantaged in knowing where and when to predict and so may have been able to initiate prediction earlier.

If participants are given an attentional demand akin to Experiment 1 but are expected to predict from the perspective of a referent within the stimuli, task relevance effects may emerge in the form of reduced and delayed predictive fixations.

Similarly, target window effects from Experiment 2, where explicitly instructed participants were less likely to fixate the target noun when it was not cued for by the verb, suggest that specifying task relevance can have downstream consequences for the integration of unpredictable information or stimuli which do not immediately fit into the task-demands (cf. Ito, 2025).
We recruited 63 participants from the same population as Experiment 1.

However, rather than being given an attention task about the Male and Female referents, participants were instead instructed to listen to each sentence and actively predict what the Male referent was doing or acting upon.

Participants had to answer, in the following order: a self-reported prediction accuracy question with "Yes" indicating that the participant's prediction of the Male referent's action was correct or "No" that it was not; a self-reported prediction confidence question, where participants were shown a Likert scale from 1 (Not confident at all) to 5 (Very confident) and asked to rate how Results for the preregistered analysis in the predictive window and target window are shown in panel C of Figure 2.

There was also a main effect of Task Group: when participants were given an explicit task to predict the actions of the Male referent, fixations to the target were more likely regardless of Condition, b = 0.346, SE = 0.079, z = 4.389, p < 0.0001.

text.text: Research on predictive processing has shown that listeners anticipate upcoming linguistic information using linguistic cues, such as verb meaning.
Beyond information in the input, listeners' prediction can also be influenced by top-down control, such as goals and strategies developed in response to a given task.
However, it is unclear to what extent evaluations of task relevance modulate top-down control of prediction.

We present evidence from two eye-tracking studies in the Visual World Paradigm that associative predictions are automatic and not influenced by implicit shifts in the task relevance of a predictive verb.

However, when a predictive verb's task relevance is made explicit in the form of an instruction to predict, prediction is upregulated and initiated earlier irrespective of the verb's predictiveness, likely due to an enhancement of predictive visual search.
Task relevance is thus modulatory for associative prediction when it is specified for listeners.

Prediction, or the "preactivation of various aspects of upcoming [linguistic] information," (Kaan & Grüter, 2021, p. 3) is a well-attested mechanism undergirding language comprehension, with listeners pre-activating upcoming linguistic input on the basis of incrementally processed cues (for overviews, see Ferreira & Chantavarin, 2018; Huettig, 2015 Huettig, , 2025;; Kuperberg & Jaeger, 2016; Magnuson, 2019).
text.formatted: Prediction, or the "preactivation of various aspects of upcoming [linguistic] information," <ref type="bibr">(Kaan & Grüter, 2021, p.</ref> 3) is a well-attested mechanism undergirding language comprehension, with listeners pre-activating upcoming linguistic input on the basis of incrementally processed cues (for overviews, see <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">Ferreira & Chantavarin, 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">Huettig, 2015</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">Huettig, , 2025;;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">Kuperberg & Jaeger, 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">Magnuson, 2019)</ref>.

text.text: These cues are present at multiple levels of representation (i.e., syntactic, lexical, phonetic, suprasegmental, discursive) and are reliably and rapidly used by comprehenders to guide predictions about upcoming input.

text.text: For example, listeners may use verb subcategorization information to predict the referent they are likely to hear next, as demonstrated in Altmann and Kamide (1999).

text.text: Using the Visual World Paradigm (VWP), Altmann and Kamide (1999) found that first language (L1) English speakers rapidly pre-activated semantic information about an upcoming object (e.g., cake) after hearing a verb (e.g., eat) which constrained for the target object, as compared to when they saw the same object with a sentence containing a non-constraining verb (e.g., move).

text.text: Similar effects have also been observed for a variety of other linguistic cues, such as verb transitivity (Arai & Keller, 2013); morphosyntactic markers of case (Mitsugi & Macwhinney, 2016), number (Koch et al., 2021), or gender (Lew-Williams & Fernald, 2007); and prosody (Weber et al., 2006).

text.text: Given the widespread and variegated use of these predictive cues, some have endorsed a view of human brains as "predictive machines" (Clark, 2013, p. 181).
text.formatted: Given the widespread and variegated use of these predictive cues, some have endorsed a view of human brains as "predictive machines" <ref type="bibr">(Clark, 2013, p. 181)</ref>.

text.text: However, this strong view of prediction as a fundamental component of human cognition and language processing is at odds with evidence that top-down factors, such as the context of prediction or a comprehender's goals and strategies, may modulate the time-course and extent of predictive behaviour (Huettig, 2015).
text.formatted: However, this strong view of prediction as a fundamental component of human cognition and language processing is at odds with evidence that top-down factors, such as the context of prediction or a comprehender's goals and strategies, may modulate the time-course and extent of predictive behaviour <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Huettig, 2015)</ref>.

text.text: Indeed, there is ample evidence that prediction is neither wholly pervasive or homogeneous, nor is it likely to be an optimal processing strategy for all populations (Federmeier, 2007; Huettig, 2015; Huettig & Mani, 2016; Kuperberg & Jaeger, 2016; Mani & Huettig, 2012; Wlotko et al., 2012).
text.formatted: Indeed, there is ample evidence that prediction is neither wholly pervasive or homogeneous, nor is it likely to be an optimal processing strategy for all populations <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Federmeier, 2007;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">Huettig, 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">Huettig & Mani, 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">Kuperberg & Jaeger, 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">Mani & Huettig, 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Wlotko et al., 2012)</ref>.

text.text: These findings motivate a top-down and forward-modeling conceptualisation of the predictive mechanism which responds to context and resource-limitations, as opposed to a ballistic, 'all or nothing' mechanism (Huettig, 2015; Wlotko & Federmeier, 2015).
text.formatted: These findings motivate a top-down and forward-modeling conceptualisation of the predictive mechanism which responds to context and resource-limitations, as opposed to a ballistic, 'all or nothing' mechanism <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Huettig, 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">Wlotko & Federmeier, 2015)</ref>.

text.text: These models of prediction center flexibility as a key feature of predictive processing while integrating resource limitations into the dynamics thereof; such resource-rational or 'resource-conscious' models (e.g., Kuperberg & Jaeger, 2016; Ryskin & Nieuwland, 2023) are moreover in harmony with recent proposals of the role of utility in guiding efficient predictive processing (Kaan & Grüter, 2021).

text.text: Since prediction may not always be necessary or cost-effective given extant resource-limitations, cue reliability, or strategies (Huettig, 2015 (Huettig, , 2025;; Huettig & Mani, 2016), considerations of utility are expected to contribute substantially to the timing and extent of predictive behaviour (Kaan & Grüter, 2021).

text.text: To explain why predictive processing displays disparate time-courses across cue types and contexts, some proposals have sought to pair resource-constrained, utility-oriented views of prediction with observable prediction behaviour under a multi-stage, multi-representational, and hierarchical architecture of language-mediated prediction (e.g., Kuperberg & Jaeger, 2016; Ryskin & Nieuwland, 2023; Salverda et al., 2011).
text.formatted: To explain why predictive processing displays disparate time-courses across cue types and contexts, some proposals have sought to pair resource-constrained, utility-oriented views of prediction with observable prediction behaviour under a multi-stage, multi-representational, and hierarchical architecture of language-mediated prediction (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">Kuperberg & Jaeger, 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Ryskin & Nieuwland, 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Salverda et al., 2011)</ref>.

text.text: One influential proposal by Pickering and Gambi (2018) argues for a two-stage model of prediction distinguishing between 'prediction-byassociation' and 'prediction-by-production' pathways (see also Pickering & Garrod, 2013).
text.formatted: One influential proposal by <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">Pickering and Gambi (2018)</ref> argues for a two-stage model of prediction distinguishing between 'prediction-byassociation' and 'prediction-by-production' pathways (see also <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">Pickering & Garrod, 2013)</ref>.

text.text: During online processing, listeners may initially utilise associations between linguistic items (i.e., functional co-occurrences) to pre-activate upcoming representations; this "general-purpose" process is presumably cost-free and requires few cognitive resources to deploy, though this may come at the expense of prediction accuracy (Pickering & Gambi, 2018 , p. 1034).

text.text: These predictions thus tend to occur earlier and may be outside of the conscious control of a comprehender to use strategically.

Prediction-by-production, by contrast, is an optional route for comprehension which is resource-intensive and involves the covert activation of mechanisms of language production (see also Pickering & Strijkers, 2025).
text.formatted: Prediction-by-production, by contrast, is an optional route for comprehension which is resource-intensive and involves the covert activation of mechanisms of language production (see also <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">Pickering & Strijkers, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Germane to the arguments presented in this paper is the extent to which top-down control guides predictive processing within these bifurcated models.

Under Pickering and Gambi (2018)'s proposed model, prediction-byassociation provides listeners with a rapid and cognitively 'cheap' track for prediction on the basis of extant semantic, functional, and phonological relations between words, with this 'fast track' supplemented by more conscious, effortful, and engaged prediction-by-production.
text.formatted: Under <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">Pickering and Gambi (2018)</ref>'s proposed model, prediction-byassociation provides listeners with a rapid and cognitively 'cheap' track for prediction on the basis of extant semantic, functional, and phonological relations between words, with this 'fast track' supplemented by more conscious, effortful, and engaged prediction-by-production.

text.text: Prediction-by-association is moreover indifferent to global top-down factors such as whether prediction is required or viable as a processing strategy, since these predictions are generated automatically and so are ostensibly beyond the scope of a comprehender's conscious control.

However, this conceptualisation of associative prediction has yet to receive a comprehensive validation, though some work has shown that associative prediction effects may be attenuated or outright inhibited when input is perceived as unreliable (Brothers et al., 2017 (Brothers et al., , 2019;; Henry et al., 2017; Hopp, 2016; Kim et al., 2026).
text.formatted: However, this conceptualisation of associative prediction has yet to receive a comprehensive validation, though some work has shown that associative prediction effects may be attenuated or outright inhibited when input is perceived as unreliable <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Brothers et al., 2017</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Brothers et al., , 2019;;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">Henry et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">Hopp, 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">Kim et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: To clarify the dynamics of prediction-by-association with respect to top-down control via strategising, we turn to studies which manipulate the task relevance of associative prediction.

We define task relevance, as it pertains to prediction, as whether linguistic information is considered relevant and consequently used for predictive processing, especially given a listener's task demands and goal.
This 'utility-driven' definition assumes linguistic representations are similarly activated but differentially used when they are task-(ir)relevant.
We distinguish this working definition from a 'mechanistic' account, which defines task relevance in terms of activation.

2 Under a mechanistic definition, task-irrelevant information (e.g., a verb and its potential associated complements) is less activated during comprehension and so is less available for prediction, even if the overall goals and strategies of the comprehender have not changed (i.e., prediction is still a goal).
Because this distinction is not a primary focus of this study, we use the phrase 'task relevance of prediction' and 'task relevance of the predictive cue' interchangeably.

Task relevance in prediction research has been most often manipulated via instructions that either explicitly upregulate prediction or which do not offer information about the viability of prediction for comprehension.

By and large, prior studies supply evidence that associative predictions proceed automatically even when it is not clear if prediction is an optimal processing strategy, with the possibility of upregulation if prediction's task relevance is clarified.

Altmann and Kamide (1999) provided early evidence of this latter possibility in the VWP: participants were asked to passively listen to sentences containing verbs which occasionally constrained for an upcoming direct object.

Participants in the passive listening group (Experiment 2) as well as those of a group asked to judge if each sentence corresponded with the visual tableau (Experiment 1) displayed prediction effects by pre-activating target information after hearing a constraining verb, suggesting that listeners generated predictions to the verbal cue irrespective of their task.
However, despite this apparent automaticity, predictive effects emerged earlier when participants had received the metalinguistic judgement task.
Although associative prediction may occur automatically or by default, additional tasks which require attending to or engaging with stimuli are likely to upregulate attention and prediction.

Importantly, this finding does not provide a complete picture of the scope of up-and downregulation possible under different task conditions and so leaves open relevant questions about the modulatory effect of task relevance.

More recent work has built on this initial finding and highlighted the influence of task relevance on the extent and time-course of predictive processing for both L1 and second language (L2) populations. Kim et al. (2026) presented 32 L1 Korean speakers with Korean sentences, some of which contained an honorific marking, while looking at a dual-image display.

text.text: Using the honorific marker, Kim et al. Kim et al. (2026) also manipulated the task relevance of the honorific cue: some participants were asked to listen to each sentence and respond to a question about the referent while others were told to actively predict the upcoming referent.

(2026)</ref> also manipulated the task relevance of the honorific cue: some participants were asked to listen to each sentence and respond to a question about the referent while others were told to actively predict the upcoming referent.

text.text: Thus, the predictive utility of the honorific cue was established as explicitly relevant to the participants' task in the latter condition, whereas it was unspecified in the former.

Both groups ultimately used the honorific cue to predict the upcoming referents, but participants who were given an explicit prediction task engaged in more robust and earlier predictive processing relative to the participants in the comprehension group. Kim et al. (2026) interpreted these results as indicative that prediction is modulated by top-down control in the form of processing goals and strategies, with listeners strategically integrating information about the relevance of the honorific cue into the predictive mechanism.

text.text: Since use of the honorific marker to predict upcoming referents necessitates Korean listeners drawing on statistical regularities and thus likely engaging in prediction-by-association (Pickering & Gambi, 2018), we take these data as evidence that associative predictions can be influenced by top-down goals and strategies so long as listeners are made explicitly aware of how a cue bears on their goals during listening.

text.text: We also note a similar study with a L1 Dutch population by Huettig and Guerra (2019) that included an explicit prediction task and reported a minor anticipatory effect when predictive, gendermarked determiner cues were presented at a naturalistic speech rate and with reduced visual preview.
text.formatted: We also note a similar study with a L1 Dutch population by <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">Huettig and Guerra (2019)</ref> that included an explicit prediction task and reported a minor anticipatory effect when predictive, gendermarked determiner cues were presented at a naturalistic speech rate and with reduced visual preview.

text.text: The authors conclude that predictive processing may be scaffolded by non-linguistic factors, such as task, but do not elaborate further on the specific role of task relevance.
Moreover, both Huettig and Guerra (2019) and Kim et al. (2026) interrogate the effect of task relevance on prediction via explicit manipulations of prediction's importance to participants' task.
text.formatted: Moreover, both <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">Huettig and Guerra (2019)</ref> and <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">Kim et al. (2026)</ref> interrogate the effect of task relevance on prediction via explicit manipulations of prediction's importance to participants' task.

text.text: Thus, current work on prediction leaves unclear whether these shifts in predictive processing also emerge when the task relevance of prediction is not explicitly clarified for listeners (i.e., under a subtle manipulation of task relevance).
Do comprehenders adjust their predictive processing as a function of task relevance without prompting or instruction, such as when task relevance is implied?

Research on L2 predictive processing has also presented evidence that language-mediated predictions are influenced by the task relevance of prediction. Ito (2025) presented 48 L2 English speakers across two studies with sentences containing objects (e.g., newspaper) that were (un)predictable based on the main verb's lexical semantics (e.g., read or buy).

text.text: In the first study, some participants were given an explicit prediction task ("predict how the sentence [is] likely to continue", p. 811) before receiving a comprehension task for a different set of stimuli.
Other participants received the opposite order.

Based on anticipatory fixations, Ito (2025) found that participants were more likely to fixate an upcoming target object which was constrained for by the verb, and that they were more likely to do so when there was an explicit prediction task.
text.formatted: Based on anticipatory fixations, <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">Ito (2025)</ref> found that participants were more likely to fixate an upcoming target object which was constrained for by the verb, and that they were more likely to do so when there was an explicit prediction task.

text.text: Despite this interaction, Ito (2025) did not report a temporal benefit for explicit prediction.

Additionally, the effects of the prediction task were likely sensitive to the order in which tasks were presented, with a potential carry-over effect of the prediction task on the comprehension block.

A follow-up experiment measured predictive fixations when participants received a comprehension task prior to the prediction task but failed to find an interaction of task and condition or any temporal difference in prediction across task conditions.

However, there was a main effect of task such that participants were more likely to fixate a target in the explicit prediction condition even when the verb was not predictive of the target. Ito (2025) thus argued that the benefit of explicit prediction tasks for predictive processing is general, with listeners using top-down strategies to upregulate predictive visual search rather than to "enhance prediction at their will" (p. 822).

text.text: A similar finding was reported in Kim et al. (2024), which utilised the same materials as Kim et al. (2026) but focused on L2 Korean speakers.
text.formatted: A similar finding was reported in <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">Kim et al. (2024)</ref>, which utilised the same materials as <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">Kim et al. (2026)</ref> but focused on L2 Korean speakers.

text.text: When L2 listeners were given an explicit prediction task, their predictive processing was comparable to that of an L1 Korean control group who had only received a comprehension task with the same stimuli.

Taken together, these two L2 prediction studies corroborate results from L1 populations (e.g., Kim et al., 2026) in suggesting that predictive processing can be upregulated when the task relevance of prediction is made explicit to comprehenders.
text.formatted: Taken together, these two L2 prediction studies corroborate results from L1 populations (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">Kim et al., 2026)</ref> in suggesting that predictive processing can be upregulated when the task relevance of prediction is made explicit to comprehenders.

text.text: However, it is unclear whether these task relevance effects require an explicit task in order to modulate predictive processing in the first place.

Additionally, we know of no study which has considered whether task relevance effects can downregulate associative prediction if listeners perceive prediction as a non-optimal strategy given an assessment of task relevance.

In addition to these questions, we consider the divergences between work on L2 and L1 prediction with respect to task relevance effects, most notably with respect to the interaction of task and predictive condition.

Ito (2025) found a more general effect of task such that predictive visual search is likely upregulated, whereas Kim et al. (2026) reported an interaction of a prediction task and predictiveness of a cue which would suggest L1 listeners can consciously and strategically enhance their use of a given cue for prediction; we return to this disparity in our overall discussion.

(2026)</ref> reported an interaction of a prediction task and predictiveness of a cue which would suggest L1 listeners can consciously and strategically enhance their use of a given cue for prediction; we return to this disparity in our overall discussion.

text.text: Synthesizing these results, we advance that there is sufficient evidence to support the conclusion that predictive processing can be upregulated when the task relevance of prediction is made explicit to listeners, such as when they are given a prediction task which clarifies the relevance of predictive processing for the task at hand.

Whether this effect is concomitant with a broader boost of predictive visual search or reflects an enhancement of more accurate prediction remains unclear, though this dichotomy may itself be affected by predictive processing in a first (or dominant) v. second (or non-dominant) language.

Importantly, prior literature corroborates a picture of predictive processing as broadly automatic (at least for associative prediction) but nevertheless situationally sensitive to top-down information (e.g., whether prediction is an ideal processing tool).
Both views endorse dynamic, resource-constrained models of prediction, which characterize prediction as malleable, resource-sensitive, and task-contingent.
Still, there is a need to qualify the pervasiveness of associative prediction and its susceptibility to top-down control.

Specifically, the current literature has not considered whether task relevance effects can emerge from listeners developing their own understanding of the relevance of prediction given a task that does not specify for them a role for prediction.
Additionally, it is unclear whether task relevance effects can work to disincentivize prediction, especially types of predictions which have traditionally been assumed to occur automatically.
That is, if a listener perceives prediction to be task-irrelevant, is there a corresponding downregulation of their predictive processing?
Such a question would also bear on resource-limitation debates as they pertain to prediction, since engagement in task-irrelevant prediction would be unexpected if anticipatory processing is costly.
To answer these questions, we present results from two experiments using eye-tracking in the VWP in which the task relevance of prediction was manipulated.
In Experiment 1, we presented participants with sentences consisting of two clauses, with one (Male or Female) referent mentioned per clause.
Experimental items contained either a predictive or non-predictive first-clause verb which constrained for one of three displayed objects and was associated with the Male referent.

Thus, by manipulating the referent to whom participants were instructed to attend, we also established a proxy manipulation of task relevance, with the predictive cue being taskirrelevant for participants attending to the Female referent.

We reasoned that if participants across attention groups demonstrated comparable predictive processing even when prediction is task-irrelevant, such findings would not support top-down modulation of prediction (e.g., resource-rational approaches).

However, if prediction effects differ across attention groups, this would provide evidence that task relevance effects can emerge under more subtle designs relative to those in past research and that prediction is sensitive to top-down mechanisms.
Experiment 2 featured the same stimuli but gave an explicit task to engage in prediction rather than an implicit manipulation of task relevance via an attentional direction.
This study acts as a direct comparison to the results of Experiment 1.
We state the following two research questions, corresponding to Experiments 1 and 2 respectively:
To what extent are predictive eye-movements affected by the implicit manipulation of the task relevance of a predictive cue, such as via an attention demand?

Are the extent and onset (e.g., increased proportions of predictive fixations, earlier predictive looks) of predictive processing sensitive to whether the predictive verb is relevant to the participant's task?
To what extent are predictive eye-movements influenced by explicit task instructions to engage in prediction?
Do listeners engage differently in predicting an upcoming target noun in terms of extent and onset when the relevance of prediction to the task is made explicit?

To respond to RQ1, we conducted an experiment with eye-tracking in the VWP in which L1 English speakers heard some sentences containing a verb constraining for an upcoming target word (a predictive verbal cue) and some sentences containing a verb which did not constrain for the target (a neutral or non-predictive verbal cue).
This target word was pictorialised alongside images of a non-target object heard in the sentence and an unrelated distractor.

To manipulate the task relevance of the predictive verbal cue, we instructed participants to pay attention to the actions of one of two referents, a Male or a Female, in each sentence for comprehension.
For Male-attending participants, their referent's actions were described by the predictive verb; for Female-attending participants, their referent's actions were not.
Thus, the prediction of the information cued by the predictive verb was always relevant to the attention task of the Maleattending group but task-irrelevant for the Female-attending group.

To ensure the task relevance manipulation was implicit to the attentional demand, both groups were only instructed to listen to each sentence and answer questions about their respective referents' actions, and neither was given specific instructions regarding prediction or was otherwise made explicitly aware of the predictive nature of the stimuli.

Given that prediction is resource-contingent (Kuperberg & Jaeger, 2016) and moreover sensitive to task relevance effects in explicit instruction designs (Kim et al., 2026), we expected listeners to display prediction effects distinct to their task demands.
text.formatted: Given that prediction is resource-contingent <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">(Kuperberg & Jaeger, 2016)</ref> and moreover sensitive to task relevance effects in explicit instruction designs <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">(Kim et al., 2026)</ref>, we expected listeners to display prediction effects distinct to their task demands.

text.text: Specifically, we predicted that when a predictive cue was not task-relevant, participants would show reduced and delayed prediction of the target image before processing of the target word in predictive sentences 3 , as well as a reduced number of target fixations while processing the target word in both predictive and non-predictive sentences.
We preregistered this experiment and its analysis on Open Science Framework (OSF) at osf.io/6qfcg.
We recruited 135 participants by word-of-mouth and from the departments of Spanish and Portuguese Studies; Speech, Language, and Hearing Sciences; and Linguistics at the University of Florida.
Participants ranged in age from 18 to 28.
Participants were required to have no issues with hearing, seeing, learning, or reading.
Participants must have also begun learning English before 6 years of age, grown up speaking English in a predominantly English-speaking country, and be comfortable speaking and reading English.
Eight participants were excluded because their eye movements could not be tracked or their data could not be extracted.
Two participants were excluded from analysis due to not fitting the language background criteria of the experiment.

Three participants were dropped for poor-quality of eye-tracking data resulting in fewer than six usable trials in either the predictive or non-predictive conditions, 1 participant was excluded for a lack of fixations in the interest areas during the predictive window, and 1 participant was removed for failing to meet the preregistered minimum for comprehension accuracy (80%).

Our preregistered analysis called for 120 participants; this number was chosen on the basis of similar sample sizes in adjacent research, as well as a preregistered power analysis estimate necessary to reach 80% power for an interaction of our factors.

Ultimately, 120 participants (age: M = 20.1, SD = 1.36) were included in the final analysis, with 57 in the Male-attending (33 self-identified as female; age: M = 20, SD = 1.1) and 63 in the Female-attending (38 self-identified as female; 2 self-identified as nonbinary; age: M = 20.1, SD = 1.56) condition.
All participants received compensation in the form of either course credit or cash at a rate of $5.00 USD per 0.5 hours.
Sessions lasted between 30 and 40 minutes.
The methods of sentence construction and image selection used in both Experiments 1 and 2 were preregistered.
Due to copyright, we are unable to share the specific images used; however, all other materials are publicly available on OSF (osf.io/63xr2) or are available upon request.
Experiment 1 followed a 2 (Condition) by 2 (Attention Group) factor design.

Sentences contained a verb whose meaning was either exclusively compatible with the target/first-clause noun (predictive) or compatible with all image-objects shown, including the second-clause noun and distractor (non-predictive).
Additionally, participants were grouped according to a betweengroup attention task.
Participants were instructed to attend to either the actions of the Male (Male-attending) or Female referent (Female-attending) and answer referent-specific questions for comprehension.

As will be discussed in greater detail below, the Attention Group manipulation serves as a proxy for a task relevance manipulation, with predictive verbs in the experimental items being task-relevant for Male-attending participants and task-irrelevant for Female-attending participants.

Sentences were bi-clausal and contained both a Male (Peter, Gary, or John) and a Female referent (Sarah, Jane, or Mary), with one referent per clause (e.g., After Gary answered his phone, Mary sighed and produced her wallet.).
In the experimental items, the Male referent always appeared in the first clause.
This first-clause verb could also be either predictive or nonpredictive of the target noun (the object of the first-clause verb), following a similar manipulation in Altmann and Kamide (1999).
text.formatted: This first-clause verb could also be either predictive or nonpredictive of the target noun (the object of the first-clause verb), following a similar manipulation in <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">Altmann and Kamide (1999)</ref>.

text.text: Thus, the target noun was always the first-clause noun in the experimental items (see Stimulus Organization).

Male-attending participants were instructed to listen to the actions of the Male referent and answer a corresponding comprehension question after each trial (e.g., What did Gary answer?) ; Female-attending participants were similarly instructed and received relevant post-trial questions (e.g., What did Mary produce?).

Since both the predictive verb and the Male referent appeared together in the first clause of the experimental items, we consider the Male-attending group the group for whom prediction was always task-relevant.

For Female-attending participants, the predictive verb (and so prediction overall) was task-irrelevant, since the Female referent was in the second clause of the experimental items and therefore not associated with the first-clause verb.

All of the images participants saw were coloured, cartoon-style clipart selected from open sources and from a set of images downloaded in 2014 from ThinkStock Photos (https://nam10.safelinks.protection.outlook.com/?url=http%3A%2F%2Fwww.thinkstockphotos.com%2F&data=05%7C02%7Cjsingleton2@ufl.edu%7Cdb3aee8dfcde4505adf408de0dc16fe7%7C0d4da0f84a314d76ace60a62331e1b84%7C0%7C0%7C638963321606780961%7CUnknown%7CTWFpbGZsb3d8eyJFbXB0eU1hcGkiOnRydWUsIlYiOiIwLjAuMDAwMCIsIlAiOiJXaW4zMiIsIkFOIjoiTWFpbCIsIldUIjoyfQ%3D%3D%7C0%7C%7C%7C&sdata=lwsNCPrVCMKRtJWSYbsv17QzUIvBZnxCPIkP5G2aiuE%3D&reserved=0) under a license held by one of the authors.

text.text: The objects were chosen such that the name of the target object did not share the initial phoneme of the non-target objects.

We did not control for any other measures of relatedness or similarity (e.g., semantic closeness, visual similarity) due to the difficulty inherent to balancing the target object being solely compatible with the predictive verb against all objects needing to be compatible with the non-predictive verb.
Note that since the displays were the same for the predictive and nonpredictive conditions, as well as for the attention groups, any difference between the groups cannot be due to the materials.
All images were adjusted to a size of 302 x 302 pixels on the computer display.
To ensure that the verbs in the predictive condition indeed elicited a preference for the target image and the non-predictive did not, we conducted a norming study.
We recruited 48 participants (age: 19 to 66, M = 33.9) on Prolific (https://www.prolific.com/) with a minimum approval rate of 80%.

text.text: This approval rate was chosen to screen for participant quality and excluded participants rejected from more than 20% of Prolific studies they have participated in.
These participants then completed the norming study in Qualtrics (https://www.qualtrics.com/).

text.text: All participants indicated that they were native English speakers, had learned English before the age of 4, and currently resided in the United States of America.

For the norming study, only the subject, verb and pre-nominal determiner of the first clause of the materials were presented alongside three pictures (target, second-clause object, unrelated distractor).
For instance, participants read Peter answered his … (predictive) or Peter lost his … (non-predictive) while viewing a picture of a phone, wallet, and glasses.
Participants were then asked to select which picture was most likely to be mentioned next in the sentence fragment.
Forty items were tested; each participant saw 20 items each in the predictive and non-predictive conditions.
Items and conditions were randomized for each participant, and three attention checks (e.g., Please select the fridge) were presented randomly.
All participants passed the attention checks.
The selection task was followed by a short questionnaire about participants' language backgrounds and whether they had been paying attention.

Based on the results of this norming study, 15 items were slightly revised and re-normed in a follow-up study with a different group of 48 raters (age: 19 to 54, M = 33.2) drawn from the same population as above.
Thirty-two pairs of items were ultimately selected for the eye-tracking study.
In these items, the target picture was selected in the predictive condition between 96% and 100% of the time (M = 99.2%), and in the nonpredictive version between 0% and 64% (M = 32.1%).
In the non-predictive condition, the second-clause object and unrelated distractor images were selected, on average, 32.1% and 35.8% of the time, respectively (for details, see osf.io/63xr2).
Sentences were recorded by a female native speaker of American English at a rate of 2.9 syllables per second using a Marantz Ò Model PMD661MKII Handheld Solid-State Recorder in a quiet room.

Audio files were subsequently edited in PRAAT (Boersma & Weenink, 2022) such that all stimuli were preceded by 100 ms of silence and the duration between first-clause verb onset and target noun onset in each item was at least 500 ms, with an overall item average between 650 and 750 ms.

text.text: This was done by lengthening the pause between the verb offset and noun onset.
The time frame from the onset of the verb to the onset of the target noun onset was longer in the non-predictive (M = 723 ms) than the predictive condition (M = 655 ms).
For this reason, we analysed our data time locked to the onset of the noun rather than the verb.
We did not specifically control for sentence length, with non-predictive sentences being slightly longer (M = 5,492 ms) than predictive ones (M = 5,129 ms).
Overall sentence length was, on average, 5,149 ms.
All sentences were normalized to 68 dB in PRAAT using a script provided by Winn (2020).

text.text: Participants were shown 68 trials in total.
Of these, 32 were experimental trials (Male referent in the first clause, Female referent in the second clause): 16 with a predictive first-clause verb, 16 with a non-predictive first-clause verb.
Participants also received 32 filler trials.

These fillers were similar to the experimental trials but crucially always contained the Female referent in the first clause. 16 of these filler trials began with a subordinating clause (e.g., While Jane was looking for a saltshaker…) while the remaining 16 contained coordinating clauses with either while, and, or but.
Sixteen of the 32 filler trials across both filler types also used a predictive verb with the Female character.
Participants also received four practice trials prior to beginning the main experimental block.
These trials were structured similarly to the experimental and filler trials but did not contain predictive verbs in either clause so as to avoid cluing participants in to the manipulation.
Experimental trials were Latin-squared over two lists per attention group such that each list contained 16 trials per condition.
Trial order was pseudorandomized.

In each trial, a sentence was coupled with a 1920 x 1200-pixel visual display containing three images (the target/first-clause, non-target/second-clause, and unrelated distractor objects) arranged around a 62 x 126-pixel centre fixation point.
Each image was positioned in one of three unique, 302 x 302-pixel interest areas and was rotated between these areas between trials to encourage eye-movement and prevent strategising.
The position of the centre fixation point was fixed and image distance from the centre was controlled to be equidistant.
