Participants were seated approximately 60 cm away from a 27-inch computer monitor with their forehead and chin on a desk-mounted headrest to minimize movement.
Eye movement data were recorded using an EyeLink 1000 desktop-mounted eye-tracker (SR Research Ltd., 2005) interfaced with an IBM-compatible PC.
text.formatted: Eye movement data were recorded using an EyeLink 1000 desktop-mounted eye-tracker <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">(SR Research Ltd., 2005)</ref> interfaced with an IBM-compatible PC.

text.text: Monocular tracking of the right pupil and corneal reflection was performed at a sampling rate of 1000 Hz.
Participants completed a 9-point calibration and validation procedure for the collection of accurate horizontal and vertical eyemovements.
Eye position errors were less than 0.5 degrees.
In the event of increased drift values or a change in the participant's posture, eye movements were recalibrated and revalidated between trials, and the reset was recorded in an experimental log.
Prior to the experiment, participants were given oral and written instructions that they would be listening to sentences while looking at objects displayed on the screen in front of them.
Participants were also instructed to attend to the actions of either the Male or the Female referent in each sentence and answer a corresponding comprehension question after each trial.
4   In between each trial, participants saw a centre fixation point.

When a fixation was detected with a drift under 0.3 degrees, the images appeared on the screen for 1,250 ms, after which the sentence was played through a pair of 5W desk-mounted Logitech Z130 PC speakers.
Answers to comprehension questions were made via mouse-click.
Prior to the main experimental block, participants saw four practice trials and could ask clarifying questions.
Participants were also able to take a break halfway through the experiment.

After the experiment, participants completed a debriefing survey and language background questionnaire via Google Forms (responses to both forms for Experiments 1 and 2 can be found on OSF; osf.io/63xr2).
All participants gave written informed consent; per regulations and policies of the Institutional Review Board of the University of Florida, the experimental protocol was exempt from review.

Prior to analysis, data for 127 participants (excluding eight participants whose data were either unextractable or not successfully collected) were subset to include only experimental trials (4,064 trials, or 7,067,296 datapoints; 2,176, 53.54%, Female-attending trials and 1,888, 46.46%, Male-attending trials).
Data were aggregated by subject and item and analysed across two separate windows: the predictive window and the target window, both time-locked to the noun onset.
We did not pre-register our analysis in the target window and present it as exploratory.
The average interval between the verb onset and the noun was 750 ms.
The predictive time window therefore spanned from 750 ms before the noun to the noun onset, offset by 200 ms (from 550 ms pre-onset to 200 ms after the noun).
We offset the window by 200 ms because planned eyemovements take approximately 200 ms to program and launch (Travis, 1936).
text.formatted: We offset the window by 200 ms because planned eyemovements take approximately 200 ms to program and launch <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">(Travis, 1936)</ref>.

text.text: The target window extended from 200 ms past the noun onset to 1,000 ms post-onset.

Data were subsequently cleaned to remove 39 trials (0.95%) containing incorrect comprehension question responses (11 of which ( 28.21%) were for Female-attending trials and 28 (71.79%) Male-attending; 17 of the 39 (43.59%) were for predictive trials and 22 ( 56.41%) were for non-predictive trials).

As well, 520 trials (12.7%) were removed for containing less than 50% usable data in the predictive window (291 ( 55.96%) Female-attending and 229 ( 44.04%) Male-attending; 257 (49.42%) had predictive verbs and 263 (50.58%) non-predictive verbs).

At the 1000 Hz sample level, we excluded blinks, saccades, and sample points suffering tracker-loss from these cleaned data (1,142,137 datapoints, (16.16%); 586,341 (51.34%) Female-attending and 555,796 (48.66%) Male-attending; 572,283 (50.11%) predictive and 569,854 (49.89%) non-predictive).

Finally, we excluded participants who had fewer than six usable trials across either level of Condition (three participants, all of whom were Female-attending), participants who had less than 80% accuracy on the comprehension questions (one participant, Male-attending), as well as participants who did not meet our inclusion criteria (two participants, both Female-attending).
One Male-attending participant was also excluded for having no looks within any interest area during the predictive window.
In total, 120 unique participants were included in the final analysis.

Pre-processed data represented 81.96% (3,331 trials) of the raw experimental subset, and data loss was approximately equivalent across conditions: Female-attending, predictive: 880 trials preserved in the pre-processed subset, 80.88% of the corresponding subcondition in the raw subset; Femaleattending, non-predictive: 869 trials, 79.87%; Male-attending, predictive: 791 trials, 83.79%; and Male-attending, non-predictive: 791 trials, 83.79%).

A generalised linear mixed effects model with family specified as binomial was run in each window using the lme4 package version 1.1-7 (Bates et al., 2014) in the R Environment for Statistical Computing program, version 4.5.1 (R Core Team, 2025).

text.text: For the dependent variable (DV), fixation data were time aligned and separated into 20 ms bins.

The total number of bins with looks to the target object versus the total number bins with looks to the secondclause and distractor objects was included as the DV in both models, with Attention Group, Condition, and their interaction serving as fixed effects.
Participant ID and Item were included as random intercepts.
We included a maximal random effects structure as justified by the design (Barr et al., 2013).
text.formatted: We included a maximal random effects structure as justified by the design <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Barr et al., 2013)</ref>.

text.text: Thus, Condition was included as a by-subject random slope with the main effects and interaction of Attention Group and Condition as by-item random slopes in both models.
All factors were deviation coded, with predictive coded as +0.5 and Male-attending as +0.5.

We also conducted an exploratory Divergence Point Analysis (DPA) using a script provided by Stone et al. (2021) and adjusted by Lago et al. (2023) to determine when looks to the target between the predictive and non-predictive conditions began to differ as a function of task relevance.

(2023)</ref> to determine when looks to the target between the predictive and non-predictive conditions began to differ as a function of task relevance.

text.text: Two generalised logistic mixed effects models with binomial distributions were fit at every sampled 20 ms bin for both attention groups with the number of bins containing target fixations versus the number of bins with non-target fixations as the DV.

To calculate the onset of group and condition-level differences, divergence points were defined as the first timepoint at which the difference in looks to the target for the predictive versus non-predictive conditions in each attention group was significant in a minimum of ten consecutive significant points (bins), or every 200 ms.
Data were sampled for N = 2000 iterations and aggregated over items and grouped by participants, bins, Attention Group, and Condition using a bootstrap function.
We then compared group onsets of target looks in the predictive condition and calculated a betweengroup prediction onset difference.
We also calculated 95% confidence intervals for the onset in both attention groups and their difference.
The DPA script, as well as the raw data and analysis pipeline, are available on OSF (osf.io/63xr2).
Comprehension accuracy was at ceiling, M = 0.99 (Male-attending M = 0.988, Female-attending M = 0.992).
Hence, participants were paying attention to their assigned referent.

Panel C shows the results of Experiment 2 for

The main aim of Experiment 1 was to determine whether the onset and extent of predictive eyemovements in the visual world were sensitive to a subtle or implicit manipulation of prediction's task relevance via an attention task (RQ1).
Participants were given an attention task that determined whether a predictive verbal cue was task-relevant (Male-attending) or task-irrelevant (Female-attending).
Based on fixations to the target object in the predictive window, we found evidence that all participants made use of the first-clause verb to predict the upcoming noun.

However, we did not find evidence of downregulated predictive processing under task-irrelevant contexts, since both attention groups were equally likely to fixate the target throughout the predictive window and began predicting at similar times.

Task relevance effects only emerged in the target window, with higher probabilities of visual attention to the target when prediction was task-relevant and regardless of whether the verb was predictive or not.
Overall, listeners engaged in prediction even when it was not required or expected of them to do so given their task-demands.
This is consistent with prior work showing predictionby-association is automatic and not influenced by top-down factors.

One potential reason for the lack of difference between the attention groups is that Female-attending participants were strategically attending to the Male referent in order to rule out the target object as a valid comprehension question answer and so converge more rapidly on the relevant object.

If Femaleattending participants began strategising during the experiment, this would imply that early in the experiment, this group would initially show predictive fixation patterns distinct from those of the Male-attending group.
However, we did not find evidence that the groups differed in their predictive processing when analysis was restricted to the first half of the data (trials one through 34; see OSF).

Alternatively, Male-attending participants may have not been aware that prediction was relevant to their task due to the instructions they received (see Footnote 4), which did not specify prediction as a task-demand or goal.
We addressed this concern in RQ2 and conducted a second experiment using the same materials in which participants received an explicit task to predict an upcoming target.
We compared these data to those of the Male-attending group in Experiment 1.
Experiment 2 presented 63 participants with the same materials and design, excepting the attention groupings, described in Experiment 1.

Crucially, these participants were given an explicit instruction task to predict, rather than simply pay attention to, the actions of the Male referent; thus, the task relevance of prediction was made explicit in Experiment 2.
To further ensure participants were maximally aware of prediction's task relevance, we also asked participants to report the accuracy and confidence of their trial-by-trial predictions.

text.text: The main aim of Experiment 2 was to test whether emphasizing the task relevance of a predictive cue through an explicit instructional demand to predict modulated the extent and time-course of predictive processing.

Experiment 1 did not find evidence of attention manipulation of task-relevance on predictive eye-movements, though this may have been due to our Male-attending participants not being aware that prediction was task-relevant.
Hence, participants in Experiment 2 were told to listen to each sentence and predict what the Male referent was doing or acting upon.

Since prediction is immediately task-relevant within this design, we predicted that participants would display faster and more frequent predictive eyemovements to the target noun compared to the Male-attending group in Experiment 1, as in Kim et al. (2026).

text.text: Altogether, we broadly corroborate extant findings for L1 prediction, though our results suggest a more general benefit for specifying the task relevance of prediction than has been previously reported.

Across two eye-tracking experiments, we examined whether the extent and onset of predictive processing is sensitive to the task relevance of a predictive cue when participants are given an attention task that renders said cue relevant or irrelevant (RQ1) or an explicit task to engage in prediction (RQ2).
Broadly, we found that prediction was sensitive to explicit manipulations of task relevance, whereas more subtle manipulations failed to modulate predictive eye-movements.

In this section, we present and interpret the overall results of Experiments 1 and 2, beginning with a corroboration of evidence that associative prediction is automatic and followed by a qualification in light of task relevance effects observed in Experiment 2.
We then motivate the findings of the explicit prediction task and offer two potential accounts favoring either a working memory-oriented or awareness-oriented explanation.
Finally, we consider limitations of the present design and avenues for future research.
We investigated effects of task relevance on the onset and extent of predictive processing in two eye-tracking experiments in the VWP.

Specifically, we tested for effects of subtle (Experiment 1, RQ1) and explicit (Experiment 2, RQ2) manipulations of task relevance while participants heard sentences containing predictive or non-predictive verbs.
In Experiment 1, the task relevance of a predictive verbal cue varied based on the referent participants were instructed to attend to.

We expected a downregulation of predictive processing when the predictive verb was task-irrelevant; however, task relevance did not influence the onset of extent of participants' associative predictions.
To test whether task relevance effects require explicit awareness, we instructed participants in Experiment 2 to actively predict the upcoming target.

In line with adjacent research (Ito, 2025; Kim et al., 2026), we found that when task relevance was specified for listeners in the form of an unambiguous prediction goal, predictive processing was upregulated.
text.formatted: In line with adjacent research <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Ito, 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">Kim et al., 2026)</ref>, we found that when task relevance was specified for listeners in the form of an unambiguous prediction goal, predictive processing was upregulated.

text.text: Critically, however, this upregulation was observed for both predictive and nonpredictive sentences, though looks in the predictive condition were initiated earlier.

We conclude from these results that associative predictions are automatic and insensitive to subtle manipulations of task-relevance, whereas specifying task relevance enhances prediction generally, possibly as a result of increased awareness, attention, or working memory resources.
Prediction is thus sensitive to top-down control, but in a limited sense.

We interpret the lack of a main effect of attended gender in the predictive window or an interaction of attended gender and condition in Experiment 1 as evidence that verbal semanticsbased predictions are likely automatic and thus outside of the strategic control of the comprehender, at least when prediction is not specifically called for.

Instead of strategically adjusting to prediction's task relevance to most efficiently process each sentence, Female-results of Experiment 2 as evidence of this initiation process, with the explicit task expediting the beginning of predictive eye-movements mostly clearly in the DPA.
Taken together, our effects in Experiments 1 and 2 provide strong evidence for the automaticity of semantic predictions and so clarify the dynamics of so-called "dumb" prediction (Huettig, 2015).

text.text: Our support for two-stage models of prediction is therefore an explication of early-stage prediction rather than a holistic analysis.

The present analysis does not offer a means to identify whether the persistence of associative prediction in Experiment 1 is directly attributable to the prediction-by-association pathway being insensitive to task relevance.
Indeed, task relevance may be defined in one of two ways, with distinct implications for our interpretation.
Under a utility-driven definition, task relevance is a measure of how integral similarly activated linguistic information is to online processing strategies.
In contrast, a mechanistic definition assumes that task-irrelevant information is under-activated and so less available for the same online processing strategies.
For the results herein, under a mechanistic definition, associative prediction may still be taskrelevant for the Female-attending group.
That is, the predictive cue may be less accessible as a result of the attention manipulation, but enough to trigger predictive eye-movements indistinguishable from those in the Male-attending group.

Our current interpretation of the results of Experiments 1 and 2 relies on a utility-driven definition of task relevance, but we are currently unable to determine whether there are in fact underlying differences in activation at the verb between the attention groups and so tease apart these two accounts of task relevance.
However, we recommend future research to more closely examine how (implicit) task relevance manipulations may influence activation during processing.
Our results from Experiment 2, when compared with those of Experiment 1, suggest that there is a general promotion of predictive processing when task-relevance is explicitly clarified.
We qualify this finding with two comments.

Firstly, explicit tasks appear to confer a general benefit for prediction which is irrespective of the cue's predictiveness, with instructed listeners deploying more frequent and earlier eye-movements to the target across predictive and nonpredictive stimuli.
These results diverge from Kim et al. (2026), who reported an interaction of predictability and task for a L1 Korean population.

text.text: However, since Kim et al. (2026) relied on a relatively simple dual image display, their reported interaction of task and predictability may have facilitated participants' predictions by reducing the domain of reference for their sentences.

text.text: Moreover, our non-predictive sentences may have also slightly benefited prediction, since some of these were slightly biased in favor of the target (see Images).
We thus cannot conclusively determine why our results diverge from those of Kim et al. (2026), but it is apparent across both studies that explicit prediction tasks can enhance predictive processing.

text.text: Conversely, our findings align with those in Ito (2025), who used a similar task manipulation and similar materials containing predictive verbs on a L2 English population.

We do note, however, a key difference across these two studies: we observe a temporal benefit for prediction, with explicitly instructed participants showing earlier anticipatory fixations to the target in the predictive versus non-predictive conditions, whereas Ito (2025) did not report significant differences in prediction onsets across task or predictability conditions.
One potential explanation is that L1/L2 predictive processing differs insofar as the former benefits more from an explicit instruction to predict.

Prediction in one's L2 is likely to be more inefficient and may be initiated later (Kaan & Grüter, 2021); an explicit prediction task thus may not suffice to overcome the gap in predictive processing ability between one's L1 and L2.

text.text: However, prediction-by-association specifically is less likely to be hindered by broader resource limitations, and so one might still expect an interaction between task and predictability even in an L2 population (e.g., Kim et al., 2024; Pickering & Gambi, 2018).
text.formatted: However, prediction-by-association specifically is less likely to be hindered by broader resource limitations, and so one might still expect an interaction between task and predictability even in an L2 population (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">Kim et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">Pickering & Gambi, 2018)</ref>.

text.text: A more likely explanation for the contrast in prediction onsets with Ito (2025) is the wording of our instructions, which were more specific about where and what listeners should predict.
text.formatted: A more likely explanation for the contrast in prediction onsets with <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">Ito (2025)</ref> is the wording of our instructions, which were more specific about where and what listeners should predict.

text.text: Ito (2025) instructed participants to "predict how the sentence was likely to continue," whereas our instructions made clear that the target was a noun serving as the direct object of a verb (see Footnote 4) (p. 11).
Consequently, our participants may have been uniquely advantaged in knowing where and when to predict and so may have been able to initiate prediction earlier.

Given that participants in Experiment 2 showed a main effect of Task Group, with the explicitly instructed participants showing more eye-movements to the target in the predictive time window than the Male-attending participants, in addition to an earlier onset of prediction for explicitly instructed listeners, we argue that these are downstream effects of enhanced predictive visual search, echoing similar arguments by Ito (2025).

text.text: That is, under an explicit demand to predict, participants begin searching for an upcoming target earlier and more widely and are thus more likely to fixate it in the predictive window.

Though we are unable to comment on the specific mechanisms powering this upregulation, one convincing account proposed by Ito (2025) is that an explicit task instruction leads to the recruitment of more working memory (WM) resources for prediction.
text.formatted: Though we are unable to comment on the specific mechanisms powering this upregulation, one convincing account proposed by <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">Ito (2025)</ref> is that an explicit task instruction leads to the recruitment of more working memory (WM) resources for prediction.

text.text: WM has been previously linked to predictive eye-movements and visual search (e.g., Huettig, Olivers, & Hartsuiker, 2011; Huettig, Rommers, & Meyer, 2011; Salverda & Altmann, 2011; Salverda et al., 2011), with listeners likely storing object-image associations in the visuospatial sketchpad to then access linguistic representations in long-term memory.
text.formatted: WM has been previously linked to predictive eye-movements and visual search (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">Huettig, Olivers, & Hartsuiker, 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">Huettig, Rommers, & Meyer, 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">Salverda & Altmann, 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Salverda et al., 2011)</ref>, with listeners likely storing object-image associations in the visuospatial sketchpad to then access linguistic representations in long-term memory.

text.text: WM resources have also been shown to influence the time-course and extent of prediction during online processing, with reduced WM capacity associated with reduced predictive processing (Huettig & Janse, 2016) and increased memory load associated with a downturn in prediction (Allison et al., 2025; Ito et al., 2018; Li & Qu, 2024; Liu et al., 2025).
text.formatted: WM resources have also been shown to influence the time-course and extent of prediction during online processing, with reduced WM capacity associated with reduced predictive processing <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Huettig & Janse, 2016)</ref> and increased memory load associated with a downturn in prediction <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Allison et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">Ito et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">Li & Qu, 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">Liu et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Thus, an explicit prediction task, by making prediction immediately task-relevant, may promote an increase in available WM resources and subsequently enhance predictive processing.
An alternative explanation of our results is that a specification of task relevance engenders a domain-general increase in awareness which is not specific to prediction (Lai et al., 2023).
text.formatted: An alternative explanation of our results is that a specification of task relevance engenders a domain-general increase in awareness which is not specific to prediction <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">(Lai et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Hence, an explicit task encourages more comprehensive and thorough utterance parsing, and so prediction may be upregulated along with other processes (e.g., integration, encoding).

This approach may explain why our effects are much more general than expected, and is moreover in harmony with findings establishing a benefit for prediction when listeners are aware, such as in learning paradigms (Andringa, 2020; Curcic et al., 2019; Koch et al., 2021).
text.formatted: This approach may explain why our effects are much more general than expected, and is moreover in harmony with findings establishing a benefit for prediction when listeners are aware, such as in learning paradigms <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Andringa, 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">Curcic et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">Koch et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Relatedly, our comparison of Experiments 1 and 2 suggests that task relevance effects may require explicit awareness to be observable, at least for associative predictions.

This finding is at least superficially at odds with descriptions of prediction as continuously updating or forwardmodeling (e.g., Brothers et al., 2017 Brothers et al., , 2019)), since we would expect listeners to adjust their predictive behaviour to how relevant prediction is at any given time-point.
text.formatted: This finding is at least superficially at odds with descriptions of prediction as continuously updating or forwardmodeling (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">Brothers et al., 2017</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">Brothers et al., , 2019))</ref>, since we would expect listeners to adjust their predictive behaviour to how relevant prediction is at any given time-point.

text.text: However, we qualify this contradiction by pointing out that the kind of prediction under study may be a poor diagnostic tool for whether listeners dynamically adjust predictive processing on account of its aforementioned automaticity.
Thus, it may appear that listeners are not sensitive to implicit or subtle task-demands only because prediction is minimally resource-intensive and so proceeds automatically.

Extending from this logic, the absence of task relevance effects in Experiment 1 as compared to Experiment 2 may implicate a level of difficulty in downregulating, rather than upregulating, associative predictions.
Such a difficulty would be expected for associative predictions if they are truly automatic, though we note the possibility that an initial goal-state could be a desire to inhibit prediction.

Some studies (Brothers et al., 2017 (Brothers et al., , 2019;; Henry et al., 2017; Hopp, 2016) have already demonstrated that prediction can be disengaged when global reliability of a cue is low, but these do not clarify whether top-down inhibition can be selfinitiated as a strategy in direct response to a task.
text.formatted: Some studies <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Brothers et al., 2017</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Brothers et al., , 2019;;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">Henry et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">Hopp, 2016)</ref> have already demonstrated that prediction can be disengaged when global reliability of a cue is low, but these do not clarify whether top-down inhibition can be selfinitiated as a strategy in direct response to a task.

text.text: Future work might clarify this dimension of associative prediction by explicitly asking participants to inhibit prediction by providing instructions similar to those in Experiment 2.
We would like to address various limitations of the present studies and suggest avenues for future research.

Firstly, as has been suggested throughout, the lack of task relevance effects in Experiment 1 may be due to the relative ease of associative predictions to the verb (Corps et al., 2022; Pickering & Gambi, 2018).
text.formatted: Firstly, as has been suggested throughout, the lack of task relevance effects in Experiment 1 may be due to the relative ease of associative predictions to the verb <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Corps et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">Pickering & Gambi, 2018)</ref>.

text.text: If the type of prediction listeners are performing is cognitively cheap, there may be no need to adjust cognitive resource distributions in response to prediction being task-irrelevant and, consequently, no need for a distinct processing strategy sans prediction.
Simply put, prediction in these two studies may be too easy.
We expect that more resource-intensive types of prediction will experience a task relevance effect, even under implicit manipulations.

Recent work by Corps et al. (2022), Corps, Liao, & Pickering (2023) and Corps, Yang, & Pickering (2023) has examined how listeners predict when they are given instructions prompting them to adopt a perspective other than their own (see also Nota et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Recent work by <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">Corps et al. (2022)</ref>, <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">Corps, Liao, & Pickering (2023)</ref> and <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">Corps, Yang, & Pickering (2023)</ref> has examined how listeners predict when they are given instructions prompting them to adopt a perspective other than their own (see also <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">Nota et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Such non-egocentric predictions have been classified as evidence of 'consistent' prediction and are generally understood to be resource-intensive.

If participants are given an attentional demand akin to Experiment 1 but are expected to predict from the perspective of a referent within the stimuli, task relevance effects may emerge in the form of reduced and delayed predictive fixations.
Such results would suggest that task relevance is involved in processing during later stages of prediction and thus align with current models of predictions.

Future research might also diversify the type of predictive cue in pursuit of more subtle and potentially effortful flavors of prediction, such as verbal cues for implicit causality (Kim & Grüter, 2021).
text.formatted: Future research might also diversify the type of predictive cue in pursuit of more subtle and potentially effortful flavors of prediction, such as verbal cues for implicit causality <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(Kim & Grüter, 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Additionally, we acknowledge that the nature of our instructions in Experiment 2 may have inadvertently biased participants to predict the target noun, potentially explaining the main effect of Task Group.

Similar studies to our own have typically presented participants with instructions that tell them to predict what will come next in an utterance without a clear indication of what participants could expect to hear or where prediction must occur (Ito, 2025; Lai et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Similar studies to our own have typically presented participants with instructions that tell them to predict what will come next in an utterance without a clear indication of what participants could expect to hear or where prediction must occur <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Ito, 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">Lai et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: By contrast, our instructions may have clued participants in to the fact that the item to be predicted was the direct object of the verb.
Thus, participants may have been better able to predict from the verb during the experiment, potentially explaining the temporal effect in Experiment 2.

Such subtle differences in instruction have yet to receive attention in the prediction literature, and future research should take efforts to investigate how instructional wording informs predictive processing.

Lastly, we should be reasonably skeptical of how informative explicit instruction designs (Experiment 2) are of processing dynamics given that naturalistic language processing is unlikely to feature overt demands to predict (Brothers et al., 2015; Huettig & Tanenhaus, 2025; Kim et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Lastly, we should be reasonably skeptical of how informative explicit instruction designs (Experiment 2) are of processing dynamics given that naturalistic language processing is unlikely to feature overt demands to predict <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Brothers et al., 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">Huettig & Tanenhaus, 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">Kim et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Considerations of task relevance may instead be pertinent at later stages of processing, such as integration.

In support of this, we point to the main effect of task relevance in the target window of Experiment 1, with Male-attending participants directing more fixations to the target noun regardless of whether it was cued for by the verb.

Since this target noun was also the answer to the post-trial comprehension question for Male-attending participants, this increase in target window fixations may reflect a strategy to integrate target information and aid comprehension.
However, the opposite argument is also possible: Female-attending participants may have been quicker to integrate the target because of its task irrelevance for following comprehension questions.
We are unable to tease these accounts apart under the current analysis but emphasize that task relevance motivates both.

Similarly, target window effects from Experiment 2, where explicitly instructed participants were less likely to fixate the target noun when it was not cued for by the verb, suggest that specifying task relevance can have downstream consequences for the integration of unpredictable information or stimuli which do not immediately fit into the task-demands (cf. Ito, 2025).
text.formatted: Similarly, target window effects from Experiment 2, where explicitly instructed participants were less likely to fixate the target noun when it was not cued for by the verb, suggest that specifying task relevance can have downstream consequences for the integration of unpredictable information or stimuli which do not immediately fit into the task-demands (cf. <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">Ito, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: We conducted two eye-tracking studies in the VWP investigating the effect of task relevance on predictive eye-movements during online sentence processing.

We found that when task relevance was modulated via an attentional demand so that prediction was task-irrelevant for certain participants, predictive processing was unhampered and proceeded similarly across attention groups.

However, when an explicit prediction task was introduced in a follow-up study, we found that participants who were given an explicit prediction task moved their eyes to the target more frequently and displayed earlier prediction effects.

From these data, we conclude that predictions based on verbal semantics are automatic and insensitive to task relevance when it is not specified and are thus best categorized as part of prediction-by-association under a two-stage model of prediction.
This type of prediction is still sensitive to top-down factors, such as goals and strategies, but only when listeners are made explicitly aware of how prediction relates to their task-demands.
Future research should investigate the extent to which this top-down control of prediction is sensitive to information about task relevance with more costly, non-automatic types of prediction.

text.text: Given that prediction is resourcecontingent (Kaan & Grüter, 2021) and that comprehenders have been shown to update their predictive behaviour in response to the utility of prediction (e.g., Henry et al., 2017), such as when predictions are routinely violated, it would be "wasteful" if listeners preactivated upcoming representations without a need to do so (Kuperberg & Jaeger, 2016, p. 44).
text.formatted: Given that prediction is resourcecontingent <ref type="bibr">(Kaan & Grüter, 2021)</ref> and that comprehenders have been shown to update their predictive behaviour in response to the utility of prediction (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">Henry et al., 2017)</ref>, such as when predictions are routinely violated, it would be "wasteful" if listeners preactivated upcoming representations without a need to do so <ref type="bibr">(Kuperberg & Jaeger, 2016, p. 44)</ref>.

text.text: However, if the type of prediction we are testing (verb-based semantic prediction) is relatively cost-free, listeners may not need to adjust predictive processing to reflect task relevance.

Such an explanation resonates with two-stage models of prediction which have distinguished between automatic and effortful processing routes (Corps et al., 2022; Corps, Liao, & Pickering, 2023; Huettig, 2015; Nota et al., 2026; Pickering & Gambi, 2018). Pickering and Gambi (2018) position the former as a minimal-cost option for predictive processing, though they note that such predictions would likely be undirected.

text.text: Thus, participants in the Female-attending group may have simply been unable to reign in their associative predictions, given that such prediction is minimally costly relative to their comprehension and attentional goals.
Therefore, we conclude in favor of an automatic view of associative prediction such that even when irrelevant to listeners' task(s), prediction persists.

Importantly, the results of Experiment 2, which indicate that associative prediction can be promoted by an explicit prediction task, are not incompatible with the view that associative prediction is automatic.

Although automatic processes are ultimately involuntary, decompositional approaches to automaticity (Mishra et al., 2013; Moors & de Houwer, 2006) have emphasized that "current, intentional goal state[s]" can initiate automatic processes, but are otherwise unable to influence the course of said processes (Mishra et al., 2013, p. 137; see also Bargh, 1994; Ito & Pickering, 2021).
